tagline.text: Siargao's Ramsar mangrove forest, where woodcutters became guardians

location.label: Location
location.text: Coastal Del Carmen, Siargao Island, Surigao del Norte

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (check the weather in the rainy and typhoon seasons)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (per person, with the boat split among 6, entrance and environmental fees and lunch included; airfare and transport within Siargao not included)

children.text: The Del Carmen Mangrove Reserve is a mangrove forest of roughly 4,800 hectares on the northwest side of Siargao Island, designated a Ramsar wetland in December 2024. The signature half-day tour takes a bangka from Del Carmen port through channels in the forest to a viewing deck and Sugba Lagoon.

Del Carmen is a municipality on the northwest coast of Siargao Island, with about 20,800 residents in 2024 and an area of about 151.68 square kilometers. Sayak Airport, Siargao's main airport, is also in this municipality. Many travelers come on tours that start from the surf town of General Luna, but the real story of Del Carmen is the wide mangrove forest that rings its coast. Local reports describe the forest as about 4,871 hectares as of 2025, the largest contiguous mangrove stand in the Philippines.

The forest survives today because of people's choices. From the 1980s Del Carmen was known as the "mangrove-cutting capital," a place where trees were cut and sold. Mangrove firewood burns long and hot, so it sold well, and of the 15 coastal barangays, 14 had mangroves and were tied up in cutting. The forest shrank from about 5,547.6 hectares in 1988 to about 4,406 hectares in 2003 and about 4,295 hectares in 2011. After a new mayor took office in 2010 and the municipal environment officer combined enforcement with persuasion, things began to change. From 2012 an NGO went from village to village holding briefings and supporting alternative livelihoods such as crab fattening, dried fish (danggit), pump boats and fish traps. A 2015 survey identified 428 people involved in cutting. Where 91 percent of the community relied on cutting in 2010, all had given it up by 2018, according to reports.

Today the forest feeds into tourism. The municipal tourism office created the mangrove tours as part of the "Siargao It Up" program, and people who once cut trees now work as boat operators and crew. Reports say 146 boat operators were registered in 2020 and more than 300 were active in 2025. The forest was designated a Ramsar wetland (Del Carmen Mangrove Reserve) in December 2024, and the conservation work is also known for winning a Galing Pook award in 2018. Residents have also said that when Super Typhoon Odette struck in December 2021, the restored mangroves blocked the waves. The conservation is the result of many groups working together. KAMAMANA, the oldest people's organization in Del Carmen, was founded in 2011 and handles planting and a nursery, and Siargao It Up began in 2013. The NGO SIKAT, active from 2012, was reported to have carried out about ₱239 million in environmental and livelihood programs across Siargao, and its field operations in Del Carmen ended in 2024. Today the municipal government, people's organizations and the sea patrol (Bantay Dagat) manage the forest together. It lies within the Siargao Island Protected Landscape and Seascape, so cutting mangroves is prohibited by law. Early on, staff were mistaken for enforcement officers and met hostility, so today's calm waterways are the result of long persuasion.

This guide is for travelers staying on Siargao who want to spend half a day or a day on the mangroves and Sugba Lagoon. The tour usually rents a boat at Del Carmen port, follows channels through the forest, passes a viewing deck and enters Sugba Lagoon, and depending on the itinerary continues to Kawhagan Island and Pamomoan beach. Fees, hours and closure dates change from year to year and amounts differ by source, so check the latest information at the local port.

Entering the narrow channels, you pass through a tunnel of mangrove roots on both sides. The usual route leaves Del Carmen port, passes through the forest, stops at a viewing deck and continues to Sugba Lagoon. Some boat operators have been involved in protecting the forest, so ask about its history and you may hear their story.
Reports describe a stop partway through the tour at a deck overlooking the whole mangrove forest. Its structure and whether it is open depend on local conditions, so check at the port.
An emerald lagoon about
20 minutes

by bangka from Del Carmen port. A floating platform on the water has a restaurant, a diving board and tables, and you can rent kayaks, paddleboards and bamboo rafts. Each visit is said to be limited to
3 hours
, and going early lets you enjoy it in relative quiet.
About
20 minutes

by bangka from Sugba Lagoon is Kawhagan Island. The sandbar that appears at low tide and a beach lunch are popular, and Pamomoan, a new beach opened in October 2019, is described as relatively quiet. The scenery changes with the tide.

According to the Ramsar information, 158 plant species and 245 animal species have been recorded in the reserve, including three threatened sea turtle species, the vulnerable Philippine duck and the southern rufous hornbill. A 2023 study reported 166 species, including 20 true mangrove species. What you actually see varies greatly with weather and tide, so it is best not to expect too much.

The story of woodcutters turned guardians is the biggest sight of this tour. In Del Carmen the municipality, villages and people's organizations restored and patrolled the forest together, and illegal cutting is reported to be at zero cases now. Hearing a resident who helped save the forest explain it as you ride changes how the scenery looks.

blocks.title: Siargao Island Protected Landscape and Seascape

children.text: The Del Carmen mangroves are part of the Siargao Island Protected Landscape and Seascape (SIPLAS). The area became a protected area by Presidential Proclamation No. 902 in 1996, and its status was reportedly strengthened in 2018 under the Expanded NIPAS Act (Republic Act 11038). Follow local guidance on the rules for the tour.

Flights operate from Manila to Siargao Sayak Airport (IAO). Airlines and timetables change every season, so check when you book.
Sayak Airport is in Del Carmen, so it is relatively close to Del Carmen port, where the mangrove tour starts. Check the exact distance locally.
Sugba Lagoon has an annual closure period. Check the closure dates before you buy airfare.
From General Luna to Del Carmen is about
45 minutes
by scooter or car. You can rent a scooter or take a tour with hotel pickup.
Rent a boat at the port and go through the forest to Sugba Lagoon.
Tricycles and motorcycle taxis run around Del Carmen town and the port.
From the port to the lagoon you can only go by bangka.

Sugba Lagoon observes a "Tourist Holiday" closure of about 32 days every year. In 2025 it ran from January 10 to February 10, and the mangrove forest tour was reported to remain open during that time. Dates may change each year.

There is lodging in Del Carmen town too, but most travelers stay in General Luna or nearby towns and make a day trip. Because the airport is in Del Carmen, if you land early in the morning you can start the tour right away. Lodging and rates change a lot by season, so check recent reviews on a booking site.

You can eat lunch at the floating-platform restaurant at the lagoon and on Kawhagan Island, with local dishes such as pork adobo and grilled fish. Restaurant staff sometimes watch the belongings on rented tables, so you can swim with peace of mind. It helps to bring water and snacks in advance. Lunch on Kawhagan Island is said to start at about ₱350, so put it in your budget.
Go to Sugba Lagoon early in the morning for fewer people and a shorter line at the diving board.
The boat fee is per boat, so filling the boat and splitting it lowers the cost per person.
Bring plenty of cash. Fees at the port and lagoon are mostly paid in cash.
The sandbar is fully exposed only at low tide, so check the tide and plan accordingly.
The sun is strong, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water, and prepare a waterproof bag.
Rent and wear a life jacket at the lagoon. Leave your belongings at the table you rent.
Do not break mangrove roots or branches or leave trash.
Ask your boat operator about the forest restoration story and the tour becomes much richer.
Ramsar designation and tour rules may change, so check the latest guidance at the port tourism office.
Sugba Lagoon closes for about a month each year, and boats may not run in bad weather. Leave room in your schedule.
Fees differ by source and by time, so the amounts in this guide are for reference. Confirm them locally.
The floating platform at the lagoon holds only about 100 people at a time, so there can be a wait during busy hours.
Always wear a life jacket on the boat, and postpone the tour on days with high waves.
Do not touch or collect plants or animals in the forest. Follow the reserve's rules.
In typhoon season, flights and boat trips may be canceled.
